Quran-Nazm · inspiration

Beautiful hand, uneven pages

Every line of the Madina Mushaf is the same width. The amount of text on those lines is not. Chapter 1 measures all 8,790 full-width lines of the 1441H print, the current King Fahd Complex edition, using its real line breaks set in a uniform digital reproduction of Uthman Taha's hand.

Page 156 · Al-Aʿrāf 44–51 · 1441H

Fifteen lines, set at their natural length

Each line below is shaped once, at one size, with no stretching. Dashed rules mark the print's line width. Red text runs past it and had to be squeezed in the print; green-tinted gaps had to be filled by stretching.

too long, compressed in printtoo short, stretched in print

Line 11 carries 10 words and runs 25% long. Line 2 carries 11 words yet runs only 2% short, and line 15 falls 15% short. Most of the page is overfull, so the print had to compress nearly every line except the last.

How the print resolved page 156

The same page in the 1441H print. Compare line 11, the longest at natural size, with line 15, the shortest: the first is visibly packed and the last is spaced out.

What fitting by scaling does to the same page

If each line is instead scaled as a whole to reach the line width, the size of the letters changes from line to line, and the pen stroke changes with it. This is a simulation of the mechanism, not a scan of the print.

Scale factors on this page range from ×0.80 to ×1.18, so the largest line is drawn 48% bigger than the smallest.

Page 72 · lines 10–12 · 1441H

The sharpest jump between neighbours

All three lines hold 9 words. Line 10 runs 11% long, line 11 falls 22% short, and line 12 runs 14% long again. Word count alone does not predict the problem; the length of the words does.

Across the whole Mushaf

Natural length of every full line relative to the fixed width. A perfectly balanced setting would put every bar at 100%.

15% of lines are more than 10% short (green) and 18% are more than 10% long (red). The middle 90% of lines span 84% to 118%.

Chapter 2 · The printed page

Uneven pen weight and texture

This chapter measures the scanned print itself: the King Fahd Complex PDF of the same 1441H edition. Each of its 15-line pages was split into lines, and every line was measured for its average pen width and for how much ink it lays down per letter. To keep the grid clean, only the 488 pages made entirely of text lines were used, 7,320 lines in all.

13%pen-width spread between a light and a heavy line (5th to 95th percentile)
9%typical spread inside a single page
50neighbouring line pairs that differ by 10% or more
1.36×spread in ink per letter

Two lines, one page, two pens

Page 102, lines 4 and 5. They sit directly on top of each other, yet the second is written with a visibly thicker stroke.

Line 5 is 16% heavier than the line above it. This is the largest jump between neighbouring lines in the measured pages.

Whole pages drift too

Average pen width per page across the Mushaf. Most pages sit in a narrow band; a few stand out. Page 561 is the heaviest page measured, about 19% heavier than page 563 two pages later.

The same line slot on two nearby pages. The difference in stroke weight is visible without measurement.

Weight follows crowding

The variation is not random. Lines that had to be stretched (short natural length) are written heavier, and crowded lines are written lighter. Pen width drops steadily from the sparsest lines to the most crowded ones.

Average pen width in px for each group of lines, grouped by how long the line's text is at natural size (Chapter 1's measure). Sparse lines average 6% thicker strokes than crowded ones.

Ink per letter shows the overall texture a reader sees: stroke weight, letter size and stretching combined. It differs even more, and it tracks crowding closely (correlation -0.61).

Ink per letter, in square pixels at scan resolution. The sparsest lines carry 31% more ink per letter than the most crowded.

The texture contrast on one page

Page 192: line 1 fits 10 words; line 14 spreads 5 words across the same width. The lower line is stretched, larger and darker, so the page does not read as one even texture.

The lower line puts 64% more ink on each letter. Part of that is elongation, part is larger, heavier letterforms.

Chapter 3 · Ayah markers

Ayahs that end on the next line

When an ayah's last word falls at the end of a line, its closing marker is often pushed to the start of the next line. The reader finishes the ayah at the far left, then meets its marker at the far right of the following line, before the next ayah begins.

This happens on 573 lines across 362 of the 604 pages. To be sure it reflects the print and not the layout data, every all-text page of the scan was checked: all 440 lines the data marks as starting with an ayah marker do start with one in the scan, and the scan shows none the data misses. Pages 533, 535 and 567 each have six such lines.

Placing the marker at a line start is an accepted convention of this print rather than an error. It is listed here because a typesetter with more freedom to stretch or compress could keep each marker with its ayah.

Method, chapter 1: line breaks and text come from the DigitalKhatt layout of the 1441H Madina print, as used in quran-madina-html v2. Each line is shaped with HarfBuzz in the QMH New Madina font with no justification features, then compared with the print's line width. Lengths are relative to this font, so they show how much each real line had to be stretched or compressed, not exact millimetres on paper.

Method, chapter 2: page images come from the King Fahd Complex PDF (archive.org item quran-madinah, 720 × 1123 px per page, about 100 ppi), whose line breaks match the 1441H layout. Each page's text frame was split into 15 equal line bands; colored ayah markers and frame elements were masked out. Each band was upsampled 4×, binarized, and measured: pen width is ink area divided by skeleton length; ink per letter is ink area divided by the line's Arabic letter count from the layout data. Pages with surah headers or basmalas were skipped. At this resolution a pen is about two pixels wide, so the numbers are best read as relative differences between lines; the sample crops show that the measured differences are visible to the eye. A higher-resolution scan would sharpen every figure.

Method, chapter 3: Line-initial markers were counted from the layout text and checked against the scan by testing whether the rightmost element of each line is a marker. Word spacing was also examined but is not reported: at this resolution, words in this hand overlap horizontally too often for blank-column measurements to separate word gaps from gaps inside words.
